subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 12! In this unit you will master two of the most useful ideas in all of mathematics: ratio and proportion. A ratio is a way of comparing quantities – how much of one thing there is for every amount of another. Proportion is what happens when you keep that relationship the same while the amounts grow or shrink. Together they let you scale a recipe up for a big Eid gathering, read the distance between Hargeisa and Berbera off a map, mix concrete in the correct strength, or share the profit from a market stall fairly between two partners.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Write and interpret a ratio using colon notation such as 3:5, and read it aloud correctly.
Explain why the order of the numbers in a ratio matters.
Tell apart part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios.
Write ratios in the same units before comparing, and simplify by dividing to the same unit.
Simplify a ratio to its lowest terms using the highest common factor (HCF), including ratios with decimals or fractions.
Find equivalent ratios and use a ratio table to solve missing-value problems.
Share a quantity in a given ratio using the parts (unitary) method.
Recognise and solve direct proportion problems using the unitary method and scaling.
Use scale and scale factors to work between map, model or drawing sizes and real sizes.

concepts.title: Understanding Ratios
concepts.explanation:
A ratio is a way of comparing two or more quantities by showing how much of one there is for every amount of another. We usually write a ratio using the colon symbol. If Farah’s flock has 3 brown goats and 5 white goats, we write the ratio of brown to white as 3:5 and read it as “three to five”. It tells us that for every 3 brown goats there are 5 white goats.

Each number in a ratio is called a term. In the ratio 3:5, the first term (3) is the number of brown goats and the second term (5) is the number of white goats. A ratio can compare more than two quantities: a concrete mix written 1:2:3 compares cement, sand and gravel all at once.

The order of the terms is not decoration – it carries meaning. The ratio 3:5 is not the same as 5:3. “Brown to white is 3:5” says there are fewer brown goats; “white to brown is 5:3” says the same flock the other way round. Always write the terms in the same order as the words in the question, and always say clearly what each term stands for. If Hassan swaps the order by accident, he ends up describing a completely different situation.

Ratios come in two useful flavours. A part-to-part ratio compares one part of a group with another part. In a class of 30 students at Nuur Academy, 12 are boys and 18 are girls, so the ratio of boys to girls is 12:18. A part-to-whole ratio compares one part with the whole group. In the same class, the ratio of boys to all students is 12:30. Notice that the whole (30) is the two parts added together: 12 + 18 = 30. Knowing which kind of ratio a question wants is half the battle, so read carefully whether it asks about a part or the total.

A ratio only makes sense when both quantities are measured in the same unit. If the units already match, we simply drop them: 6 metres to 9 metres is just 6:9. But if the units differ, you must convert to a common unit before writing the ratio. Compare 2 hours to 90 minutes: change the hours to minutes first, so 2 hours = 120 minutes, giving 120 minutes : 90 minutes = 120:90, which simplifies to 4:3. If Omar forgets to convert and writes 2:90, he has compared apples with mangoes and his ratio is meaningless.
concepts.example: Because a ratio compares quantities in the same unit, it has no units of its own – it is a pure comparison of size. This is exactly why a ratio can be written as a fraction: 3:5 is closely linked to the fraction 3/5, and this connection will help us simplify ratios and solve proportions later.

concepts.title: Simplifying Ratios
concepts.explanation:
To simplify a ratio means to write it using the smallest possible whole numbers while keeping exactly the same relationship. It works just like simplifying a fraction: you divide every term by the highest common factor (HCF) – the largest number that divides into all the terms exactly.

Let us simplify 12:18 step by step. First list the factors: the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, and the factors of 18 are 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The common factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6, so the HCF is 6. Now divide both terms by 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, giving 2:3. The ratio 2:3 is much clearer than 12:18, yet it describes exactly the same relationship.

Here is the reliable method to follow every time:

Make sure all the terms are in the same unit.

Write the simplified ratio and check that no number still divides into all the terms.

The same method works with three terms. To simplify 24:36:48, the HCF of 24, 36 and 48 is 12, so we divide each term by 12 to get (24÷12):(36÷12):(48÷12) = 2:3:4. Always divide every term by the same number, or you will change the relationship.

When a ratio contains decimals, first multiply every term by the same power of ten to clear the decimals, then simplify as usual. To simplify 1.5:2.5, multiply both terms by 10 to get 15:25. The HCF of 15 and 25 is 5, so 15:25 = 3:5. Multiplying both terms by the same number does not change the ratio – it is the same trick as making equivalent fractions.

When a ratio contains fractions, multiply every term by the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the denominators to clear the fractions, then simplify. To simplify 1/2 : 2/3 : 3/4, the LCM of 2, 3 and 4 is 12. Multiply every term by 12: (1/2×12):(2/3×12):(3/4×12) = 6:8:9. The terms 6, 8 and 9 share no common factor greater than 1, so 6:8:9 is already in its simplest form.
concepts.example: Why bother simplifying at all? A simplified ratio is easier to understand, easier to compare with another ratio, and easier to use in a calculation. The ratio 2:3 communicates the relationship far more clearly than 14:21, even though the two are equivalent. Whenever you finish a ratio problem, simplifying your answer is the polite, professional final step.

concepts.title: Equivalent Ratios and Ratio Tables
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent ratios describe the same relationship using different numbers, just as equivalent fractions describe the same portion of a whole. The ratios 2:3, 4:6, 6:9 and 8:12 are all equivalent because they all simplify to 2:3. To build an equivalent ratio, you multiply or divide every term by the same non-zero number.

Starting from 3:5, multiply both terms by 2 to get 6:10, by 3 to get 9:15, and by 4 to get 12:20. Every one of these is equivalent to 3:5. Going the other way, dividing both terms of 12:20 by 4 brings you back to 3:5. Multiplying scales the relationship up; dividing scales it back down.

Testing Whether Two Ratios Are Equivalent

There are three neat ways to test whether two ratios are equivalent. First, simplify both and see if they match: 6:9 simplifies to 2:3 and 8:12 also simplifies to 2:3, so they are equivalent. Second, use cross multiplication – for a:b and c:d, they are equivalent when a×d = b×c. Testing 4:6 against 10:15 gives 4×15 = 60 and 6×10 = 60; since both are 60, they are equivalent. Third, turn each into a fraction and compare: 4:6 = 4/6 = 2/3 and 10:15 = 10/15 = 2/3, so they match. Choose whichever method feels quickest for the numbers in front of you.

A ratio table lines up equivalent ratios in neat columns so you can read off missing values easily. Suppose a bariis recipe uses flour and sugar in the ratio 3:2. Each row of the table below keeps that same 3:2 relationship, scaled up step by step. If you know one quantity, you can find its partner by looking across the row.
concepts.example: Equivalent ratios are the key to solving missing-value problems. Suppose the recipe keeps flour to sugar at 3:2, and Khadija uses 9 cups of flour – how much sugar does she need? Set up equivalent ratios 3:2 = 9:?. Since 3 was multiplied by 3 to reach 9, multiply the sugar term by 3 as well: 2×3 = 6 cups of sugar. Whatever you do to one term, do to the other, and the relationship stays true.

concepts.title: Sharing a Quantity in a Given Ratio
concepts.explanation:
One of the most useful things you can do with a ratio is share an amount fairly. Suppose Aisha and Ibrahim run a market stall together and share the day’s profit of 240 shillings in the ratio 3:5, because Ibrahim worked more hours. How much does each person get? The parts method makes this simple and safe.

Here is the method, which always works:

Add the terms of the ratio to find the total number of parts: 3 + 5 = 8 parts.

Divide the amount by the total parts to find the value of one part: 240 ÷ 8 = 30 shillings per part.

Multiply each term by the value of one part: Aisha gets 3 × 30 = 90, and Ibrahim gets 5 × 30 = 150.

Check by adding the shares back together: 90 + 150 = 240. It matches the total, so the answer is correct.

That checking step in the last line is worth its weight in gold. Because the two shares must add back to the original amount, you can always test your own answer. If Aisha’s and Ibrahim’s shares did not add up to 240, you would know at once that a slip had crept in.

The same method handles three-way sharing. A concrete mix uses cement, sand and gravel in the ratio 1:2:3, and Yusuf needs 12 cubic metres of concrete in total. Add the parts: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 parts. One part is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 cubic metres. So cement = 1×2 = 2, sand = 2×2 = 4, and gravel = 3×2 = 6 cubic metres. Check: 2 + 4 + 6 = 12. Perfect.
concepts.example: Always begin sharing problems by finding the total number of parts, because the amount is being divided into that many equal parts. A very common slip is to divide by one of the terms instead of by the total – always add the terms first.

concepts.title: Direct Proportion and the Unitary Method
concepts.explanation:
A proportion is simply a statement that two ratios are equal, such as 2:3 = 6:9. Two quantities are in direct proportion when they grow together at the same rate: as one doubles, so does the other; as one halves, so does the other. The cost of mangoes is in direct proportion to how many you buy (at a fixed price each). The distance a bus travels is in direct proportion to the time it drives (at a steady speed). In every case the ratio between the two quantities stays constant.

The most powerful tool for direct proportion is the unitary method: find the value of one unit first, then multiply up to however many you need. The word ‘unitary’ comes from ‘unit’, meaning one. This single idea solves an enormous range of everyday problems.

Worked Idea: Using the Unitary Method

Suppose 5 pencils cost 15 shillings, and Sahra wants to know the cost of 8 pencils. First find the cost of one pencil: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 shillings each. Now multiply up for 8 pencils: 8 × 3 = 24 shillings. Find one, then scale – that is the whole method in five words.

You can also solve direct proportion by scaling with a factor. A recipe for 4 people uses 2 cups of flour; how much flour serves 10 people? The scaling factor is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5, so scale the flour: 2 × 2.5 = 5 cups. Whether you find one unit first or multiply by a scaling factor, you are keeping the ratio constant – both routes reach the same answer, so use whichever is easier for the numbers you have.

Proportion is exactly how money is exchanged. Suppose 1 US dollar = 135 shillings. How many shillings does Idris get for 50 dollars? The value of one unit (one dollar) is already given as 135 shillings, so multiply up: 50 × 135 = 6 750 shillings. Exchange rates are proportion in action, which is why the same reasoning also handles medicine doses, fuel costs and wages.
concepts.example: One caution: not every relationship is direct proportion. If a relationship is direct, then when one quantity is zero the other must be zero too (zero pencils cost zero shillings), and doubling one always doubles the other. If doubling one quantity does not double the other, the quantities are not in direct proportion, and the unitary method will not apply. Always sanity-check that the story really does grow at a constant rate.

concepts.title: Scale, Maps and Scale Factors
concepts.explanation:
Scale is a special use of ratio that compares the size of a map, drawing or model with the real object it represents. A scale lets us show something enormous, like the road between two cities, on a small sheet of paper, or something tiny in a larger, clearer drawing. A map scale of 1:50 000 means that 1 unit on the map stands for 50 000 of the same units in real life.

A scale factor tells you how many times bigger or smaller one figure is than another. If a model car is built at a scale of 1:50, then every real length is 50 times the model length. So if the real car is 4 metres long, the model is 4 ÷ 50 = 0.08 metres = 8 cm long. A scale factor greater than 1 gives an enlargement; a scale factor less than 1 gives a reduction; a scale factor of exactly 1 leaves the size unchanged.

Maps turn scale into a practical skill. On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm on the paper represents 50 000 cm in reality. Since 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km, every centimetre on this map is half a kilometre on the ground. To find a real distance, measure the map distance and multiply by the scale. If Hargeisa and a nearby town are 3 cm apart on the map, the real distance is 3 × 50 000 = 150 000 cm = 1.5 km. To work the other way – from real distance to map distance – you divide by the scale instead.

Architects and engineers rely on precise scales. A floor plan drawn at 1:100 means 1 cm on the plan is 1 metre in the real building; a detailed drawing at 1:50 means 1 cm is half a metre. The rule is always the same: real size = drawing size × scale, and drawing size = real size ÷ scale. Keep your units consistent throughout, convert carefully at the end, and scale problems become straightforward arithmetic.

A useful warning: a scale factor applies to lengths. When shapes are enlarged, areas and volumes grow much faster than lengths – but for this unit, focus on getting lengths, map distances and model sizes right using the multiply-or-divide rule above.

You have now met six big ideas: writing and interpreting ratios, simplifying them, finding equivalent ratios with a table, sharing an amount in a given ratio, solving direct proportion with the unitary method, and working with scale and scale factors. These ideas are not separate islands – they support one another. When Amina scales a recipe, she is using equivalent ratios and the unitary method at once. When Yusuf reads a map, he is using a ratio (the scale) as a proportion. When Aisha and Ibrahim split their profit, they simplify a ratio and then share by parts.
concepts.example: The secret to mastering this unit is to notice the same core move again and again: keep the ratio constant. Whether you multiply both terms, divide by the HCF, find the value of one unit, or scale a map distance, you are always protecting that fixed relationship between the quantities. Once you truly see that single idea running through every method, ratio and proportion stop being a list of tricks and become one clear way of thinking. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to simplify a ratio
methods.example: In a class of 30 students, 12 are boys and 18 are girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form.
steps: Make sure all terms are in the same unit.
Find the HCF of all the terms.
Divide every term by the HCF.
Check that no number still divides into all the terms.

methods.title: How to share an amount in a ratio
methods.example: Write the ratio of 2 hours to 90 minutes in its simplest form.
steps: Add the terms to find the total number of parts.
Divide the amount by the total parts to find one part.
Multiply each term by the value of one part.
Check by adding all the shares back to the original amount.

methods.title: How to solve direct proportion (unitary method)
steps: Find the value of one unit by dividing.
Multiply by the number of units you want.
Check the answer makes sense in the real situation.

methods.title: Find a missing value
methods.example: The ratio of flour to sugar is 3:2. Farah uses 9 cups of flour. How much sugar does she need?
steps: Set up equivalent ratios 3:2 = 9:?.
Since 3 was multiplied by 3 to give 9, multiply the sugar term by 3 as well: 2 × 3 = 6 cups of sugar.
Check your ratio is still equivalent: 9:6 should simplify back to 3:2.

methods.title: Share in a ratio
methods.example: Aisha and Ibrahim share 240 shillings in the ratio 3:5. How much does each get?
steps: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8.
One part = 240 ÷ 8 = 30 shillings.
Aisha gets 3 × 30 = 90; Ibrahim gets 5 × 30 = 150.

methods.title: The unitary method
methods.example: If 5 pencils cost 15 shillings, how much do 8 pencils cost?
steps: Cost of one pencil = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 shillings.
Cost of 8 pencils = 8 × 3 = 24 shillings.
Check by dividing your final answer by 8 — it should return the cost of one pencil, 3 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Write and simplify a ratio
workedExamples.prompt: In a class of 30 students, 12 are boys and 18 are girls. Write the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form.
workedExamples.solution: The ratio of boys to girls is 12:18. The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6, so divide both terms by 6: (12÷6):(18÷6) = 2:3. For every 2 boys there are 3 girls.

workedExamples.title: Ratio with different units
workedExamples.prompt: Write the ratio of 2 hours to 90 minutes in its simplest form.
workedExamples.solution: First make the units match. 2 hours = 120 minutes, so the ratio is 120:90. The HCF of 120 and 90 is 30, so (120÷30):(90÷30) = 4:3.

workedExamples.title: Clear the decimals
workedExamples.solution: Multiply both terms by 10 to clear the decimals: 15:25. The HCF of 15 and 25 is 5, so (15÷5):(25÷5) = 3:5.

workedExamples.title: Find a missing value
workedExamples.prompt: The ratio of flour to sugar is 3:2. Farah uses 9 cups of flour. How much sugar does she need?
workedExamples.solution: Set up equivalent ratios 3:2 = 9:?. Since 3 was multiplied by 3 to give 9, multiply the sugar term by 3 as well: 2 × 3 = 6 cups of sugar.

workedExamples.title: Share in a ratio
workedExamples.prompt: Aisha and Ibrahim share 240 shillings in the ratio 3:5. How much does each get?
workedExamples.solution: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8. One part = 240 ÷ 8 = 30 shillings. Aisha gets 3 × 30 = 90; Ibrahim gets 5 × 30 = 150. Check: 90 + 150 = 240. Correct.

workedExamples.title: The unitary method
workedExamples.prompt: If 5 pencils cost 15 shillings, how much do 8 pencils cost?
workedExamples.solution: Cost of one pencil = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 shillings. Cost of 8 pencils = 8 × 3 = 24 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Sum and ratio together
workedExamples.prompt: Two numbers are in the ratio 7:4, and their sum is 66. Find the two numbers.
workedExamples.solution: Total parts = 7 + 4 = 11. One part = 66 ÷ 11 = 6. The numbers are 7 × 6 = 42 and 4 × 6 = 24. Check: 42 + 24 = 66. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Map scale
workedExamples.prompt: Two towns are 3 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map. What is the real distance in kilometres?
workedExamples.solution: Real distance = 3 × 50 000 = 150 000 cm. Convert: 150 000 cm = 1 500 m = 1.5 km.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: If 6 sambusas cost 30 shillings, how much do 10 sambusas cost?
workedExamples.solution: One sambusa costs 30 ÷ 6 = 5 shillings. Ten sambusas cost 10 × 5 = 50 shillings.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: A recipe for 4 people uses 2 cups of rice. How much rice is needed for 10 people?
workedExamples.solution: The scale factor from 4 to 10 people is 10 ÷ 4 = 2.5. Multiply the rice by the same factor: 2 × 2.5 = 5 cups of rice.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: The ratio of red to blue beads is 3:7. There are 21 red beads. How many blue beads and how many beads in total?
workedExamples.solution: One part = 21 ÷ 3 = 7 beads. Blue beads = 7 × 7 = 49. Total beads = 21 + 49 = 70.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Two numbers are in the ratio 5:3 and their difference is 16. Find the two numbers.
workedExamples.solution: Difference is 5 − 3 = 2 parts = 16, so one part = 8; numbers are 40 and 24.

activities.title: The Perfect Juice Mix
activities.materials: cups, water, and a squash, juice or milk you like.
steps: Choose a mixing ratio, for example 1 part juice to 4 parts water (1:4).
Measure out 1 cup of juice and 4 cups of water and stir.
Now double the drink for more guests: use 2 cups of juice and 8 cups of water. Notice the ratio stays 1:4.
Try a stronger mix, such as 1:3, and taste the difference. Which ratio do your family prefer?
This shows how equivalent ratios keep the same taste even when you make more.

activities.title: Scale Up the Recipe (Family Cooking)
activities.materials: a simple recipe (bariis, anjero or a cake) and a family member to cook with.
steps: Find a recipe and note how many people it serves.
Count how many people you actually want to feed and work out the scaling factor.
Multiply every ingredient by the scaling factor and write the new amounts.
Cook it together and check that the food still tastes right – proof that proportion works!

activities.title: Fair Shares Game
activities.materials: a pile of counters, dried beans, stones or dates.
steps: Count out a total, for example 40 beans.
Pick a sharing ratio such as 3:5 and add the parts: 3 + 5 = 8.
Find one part (40 ÷ 8 = 5) and deal out the two shares (15 and 25).
Check the shares add back to the total, then try new totals and ratios.
This is exactly how market partners split their profit fairly.

activities.title: Map Distance Investigation
activities.materials: a printed or drawn map with a scale, and a ruler.
steps: Find the scale printed on the map, for example 1:50 000.
Measure the straight distance between two places in centimetres.
Multiply by the scale to find the real distance, then convert to kilometres.
Check three different pairs of places and record your results in a small table.

activities.title: Build a Scale Model
activities.materials: paper, a ruler, and something to measure such as a table or a room.
steps: Measure the real length and width of a table or room in centimetres.
Choose a scale factor, for example 1:20, so every real length is divided by 20.
Draw the scaled rectangle on paper using your calculated measurements.
Add scaled furniture and label each length. How realistic does your plan look?

activities.title: Ratio Hunt (Investigation)
activities.materials: a notebook and your everyday surroundings.
steps: Spend one day spotting ratios around you: goats to sheep, boys to girls, price of two items.
Write down at least five real ratios you find.
Simplify each ratio to its lowest terms.
Share your list with your teacher and explain what each ratio compares.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand ratio and proportion best? Where did you see a constant ratio staying the same as amounts grew? What was the trickiest part, and what would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Ratio Basics
rules.text: A ratio compares quantities in the same unit, written with a colon, e.g. 3:5. Order matters: 3:5 is not the same as 5:3. Convert to the same unit before writing or simplifying a ratio.

rules.title: Simplifying Rule
rules.text: Divide every term by the highest common factor (HCF). Clear decimals by multiplying by 10, 100, and so on, then simplify. Clear fractions by multiplying by the LCM of the denominators, then simplify.

rules.title: Sharing Rule
rules.text: Add the terms to get the total number of parts. Divide the amount by the total parts to find one part. Multiply each term by one part; check the shares add to the total.

rules.title: Proportion and Scale Rule
rules.text: Unitary method: find the value of one unit, then multiply up. Real size = drawing or map size multiplied by the scale. Drawing or map size = real size divided by the scale.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Direct Proportion and the Unitary Method.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A proportion is simply a statement that two ratios are equal, such as 2:3 = 6:9. Two quantities are in direct proportion when they grow together at the same rate: as one doubles, so does the other; as one halves, so does the other. The cost of mangoes is in direct proportion to how many you buy (at a fixed price each). The distance a bus travels is in direct proportion to the time it drives (at a steady speed). In every case the ratio between the two quantities stays constant. The most powerful tool for direct proportion problems is the unitary method: find the value of one unit first, then multiply to find the value you need. For example, if 5 pencils cost 15 shillings, one pencil costs 15 ÷ 5 = 3 shillings, so 8 pencils cost 8 × 3 = 24 shillings.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Scale, Maps and Scale Factors.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Scale is a special use of ratio that compares the size of a map, drawing or model with the real object it represents. A scale lets us show something enormous, like the road between two cities, on a small sheet of paper, or something tiny in a larger, clearer drawing. A map scale of 1:50 000 means that 1 unit on the map stands for 50 000 of the same units in real life. A scale factor tells you how many times bigger or smaller one figure is than another. If a model car is built at a scale of 1:50, then every real length on the car is 50 times the matching length on the model. To find the real size, multiply the model or map size by the scale factor; to find the model or map size, divide the real size by the scale factor.

rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Multiply both terms by 10 to clear the decimals: 4:16. The HCF of 4 and 16 is 4, so 4:16 = 1:4.

rounds.prompt: Write the ratio of 3 hours to 45 minutes in its simplest form.
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Convert to the same unit first: 3 hours = 180 minutes, so 180:45 = 4:1.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Simplify
games.description: Practise simplify through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Term” mean?
choices: One of the numbers in a ratio
Divide all terms by the HCF
Different ratios showing the same relationship
A statement that two ratios are equal
rounds.answer: One of the numbers in a ratio
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 12 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Term means One of the numbers in a ratio.

rounds.prompt: The ratio 4:5 is equivalent to 20:?. What is the missing number?
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: 4 was multiplied by 5 to get 20, so multiply 5 by 5 as well: 5 × 5 = 25.

rounds.prompt: Share 40 sweets between two children in the ratio 3:5. How many sweets does the second child get?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8. One part = 40 ÷ 8 = 5. The second child gets 5 × 5 = 25 sweets.

rounds.prompt: If 4 kilograms of rice cost 320 shillings, how much do 7 kilograms cost?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: One kilogram costs 320 ÷ 4 = 80 shillings, so 7 kilograms cost 7 × 80 = 560 shillings.

games.description: Practise equivalent ratios through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Simplify” mean?
choices: Divide all terms by the HCF
Different ratios showing the same relationship
A statement that two ratios are equal
Both quantities grow at the same rate
rounds.answer: Divide all terms by the HCF
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 12 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Simplify means Divide all terms by the HCF.

rounds.prompt: A necklace has 4 red beads and 6 blue beads, 10 beads in total. Which ratio compares red beads to ALL the beads (part-to-whole)?
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Part-to-whole compares one part to the total: 4 red beads out of 10 beads altogether is 4:10.

rounds.prompt: The ratio of boys to girls in a class is 3:5. What does the ratio 5:3 describe instead?
choices: Girls to boys
Boys to girls
The total number of students
The number of boys only
rounds.answer: Girls to boys
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Swapping the order of a ratio reverses what is being compared: 5:3 means girls to boys, not boys to girls.

rounds.prompt: A recipe ratio is written as 2:7. Which statement correctly interprets this ratio?
choices: For every 2 parts of the first ingredient there are 7 parts of the second
There are 9 parts of the first ingredient
The two ingredients are in equal amounts
The second ingredient is 2 times the first
rounds.answer: For every 2 parts of the first ingredient there are 7 parts of the second
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: A ratio of 2:7 means that for every 2 parts of the first quantity there are 7 parts of the second quantity.

selfAssessment: I can write and interpret a ratio using colon notation such as 3:5, and read it aloud correctly.
I can explain why the order of the numbers in a ratio matters.
I can tell apart part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios.
I can write ratios in the same units before comparing, and simplify by dividing to the same unit.
I can simplify a ratio to its lowest terms using the highest common factor (HCF), including ratios with decimals or fractions.
I can find equivalent ratios and use a ratio table to solve missing-value problems.
I can share a quantity in a given ratio using the parts (unitary) method.
I can recognise and solve direct proportion problems using the unitary method and scaling.
I can use scale and scale factors to work between map, model or drawing sizes and real sizes.
